In [[probability theory]] and [[statistics]], the '''noncentral chi-squared distribution''' (or noncentral chi-square distribution, '''noncentral <math>\chi^2</math> distribution''') is a [[noncentral distribution|noncentral generalization]] of the [[chi-squared distribution]].  It often arises in the [[statistical power|power analysis]] of statistical tests in which the null distribution is (perhaps asymptotically) a chi-squared distribution; important examples of such tests are the [[likelihood-ratio test]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Patnaik |first=P. B. |date=1949 |title=The Non-Central χ2- and F-Distribution and their Applications |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2332542 |journal=Biometrika |volume=36 |issue=1/2 |pages=202–232 |doi=10.2307/2332542 |jstor=2332542 |issn=0006-3444|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Definitions ==
=== Background ===
Let <math>(X_1,X_2, \ldots, X_i, \ldots,X_k)</math> be ''k'' [[statistical independence|independent]], [[normal distribution|normally distributed]] random variables with means <math>\mu_i</math> and unit variances. Then the random variable

: <math>\sum_{i=1}^k X_i^2</math>

is distributed according to the noncentral chi-squared distribution. It has two parameters: <math>k</math> which specifies the number of [[Degrees of freedom (statistics)|degrees of freedom]] (i.e. the number of <math>X_i</math>), and <math>\lambda</math> which is related to the mean of the random variables <math>X_i</math> by:

: <math>\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^k \mu_i^2.</math>

<math>\lambda</math> is sometimes called the [[noncentrality parameter]]. Note that some references define <math>\lambda</math> in other ways, such as half of the above sum, or its square root.

This distribution arises in [[multivariate statistics]] as a derivative of the [[multivariate normal distribution]]. While the central [[chi-squared distribution]] is the squared [[Euclidean distance|norm]] of a [[random vector]] with <math>N(0_k,I_k)</math> distribution (i.e., the squared distance from the origin to a point taken at random from that distribution), the non-central <math>\chi^2</math> is the squared norm of a random vector with <math>N(\mu,I_k)</math> distribution. Here <math>0_k</math> is a zero vector of length ''k'', <math>\mu = (\mu_1, \ldots, \mu_k)</math> and <math>I_k</math> is the [[identity matrix]] of size ''k''.

=== Density ===
The [[probability density function]] (pdf) is given by
:<math>
f_X(x; k,\lambda) = \sum_{i=0}^\infty \frac{e^{-\lambda/2} (\lambda/2)^i}{i!} f_{Y_{k+2i}}(x),
</math>
where <math>Y_q</math> is distributed as chi-squared with <math>q</math> degrees of freedom.

From this representation, the noncentral chi-squared distribution is seen to be a Poisson-weighted [[mixture density|mixture]] of central chi-squared distributions. Suppose that a random variable ''J'' has a [[Poisson distribution]] with mean <math>\lambda/2</math>, and the [[conditional distribution]] of ''Z'' given ''J''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''i'' is chi-squared with ''k''&nbsp;+&nbsp;2''i'' degrees of freedom. Then the [[marginal distribution|unconditional distribution]] of ''Z'' is non-central chi-squared with ''k'' degrees of freedom, and non-centrality parameter <math>\lambda</math>.

Alternatively, the pdf can be written as
: <math>f_X(x;k,\lambda)=\frac 1 2 e^{-(x+\lambda)/2} \left (\frac x \lambda \right)^{k/4-1/2} I_{k/2-1}(\sqrt{\lambda x})</math>

where <math>I_\nu(y)</math> is a [[Bessel function#Modified Bessel functions|modified Bessel function]] of the first kind given by

:<math> I_\nu(y) = (y/2)^\nu \sum_{j=0}^\infty \frac{ (y^2/4)^j}{j! \Gamma(\nu+j+1)}. </math>

Using the relation between [[Bessel function]]s and [[hypergeometric functions]], the pdf can also be written as:<ref>Muirhead (2005) Theorem 1.3.4</ref>

:<math>f_X(x;k,\lambda)={{\rm e}^{-\lambda/2}} _0F_1(;k/2;\lambda x/4)\frac 1 {2^{k/2} \Gamma(k/2)} {\rm e}^{-x/2} x^{k/2-1}.</math>

The case ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 ([[zero degrees of freedom]]), in which case the distribution has a discrete component at zero, is discussed by Torgersen (1972) and further by Siegel (1979).<ref>Torgersen, E. N. (1972), "Supplementary notes on linear models", Preprint series: Statistical Memoirs, Dept. of Mathematics, University of Oslo, http://urn.nb.no/URN:NBN:no-58681</ref><ref>Siegel, A. F. (1979), "The noncentral chi-squared distribution with zero degrees of freedom and testing for uniformity", ''[[Biometrika]]'', 66, 381–386</ref>

=== Derivation of the pdf ===
The derivation of the probability density function is most easily done by performing the following steps:

# Since <math>X_1,\ldots,X_k</math> have unit variances, their joint distribution is spherically symmetric, up to a location shift.
# The spherical symmetry then implies that the distribution of <math>X=X_1^2+\cdots+X_k^2</math> depends on the means only through the squared length, <math>\lambda=\mu_1^2+\cdots+\mu_k^2</math>. Without loss of generality, we can therefore take <math>\mu_1=\sqrt{\lambda}</math> and <math>\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k=0</math>.
# Now derive the density of <math>X=X_1^2</math> (i.e. the ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 case). Simple transformation of random variables shows that
:::<math>\begin{align}f_X(x,1,\lambda) &= \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\left( \phi(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{\lambda}) + \phi(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{\lambda}) \right )\\ &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi x}} e^{-(x+\lambda)/2} \cosh(\sqrt{\lambda x}), \end{align}</math>
::where <math>\phi(\cdot)</math> is the standard normal density.
# Expand the [[hyperbolic function|cosh]] term in a [[Taylor series]]. This gives the Poisson-weighted mixture representation of the density, still for ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1. The indices on the chi-squared random variables in the series above are 1&nbsp;+&nbsp;2''i'' in this case.
# Finally, for the general case. We've assumed, without loss of generality, that <math>X_2,\ldots,X_k</math> are standard normal, and so <math>X_2^2+\cdots+X_k^2</math> has a ''central'' chi-squared distribution with (''k''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1) degrees of freedom, independent of <math>X_1^2</math>. Using the poisson-weighted mixture representation for <math>X_1^2</math>, and the fact that the sum of chi-squared random variables is also a chi-square, completes the result. The indices in the series are (1&nbsp;+&nbsp;2''i'')&nbsp;+&nbsp;(''k''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1) =&nbsp;''k''&nbsp;+&nbsp;2''i'' as required.

== Properties ==
=== Moment generating function ===
The [[moment-generating function]] is given by

:<math>M(t;k,\lambda)=\frac{\exp\left(\frac{ \lambda t}{1-2t }\right)}{(1-2 t)^{k/2}}.</math>

=== Moments ===
The first few raw [[moment (mathematics)|moments]] are:

:<math>\mu'_1=k+\lambda</math>
:<math>\mu'_2=(k+\lambda)^2 + 2(k + 2\lambda) </math>
:<math>\mu'_3=(k+\lambda)^3 + 6(k+\lambda)(k+2\lambda)+8(k+3\lambda)</math>
:<math>\mu'_4=(k+\lambda)^4+12(k+\lambda)^2(k+2\lambda)+4(11k^2+44k\lambda+36\lambda^2)+48(k+4\lambda).</math>

The first few central [[moment (mathematics)|moments]] are:

:<math>\mu_2=2(k+2\lambda)\,</math>
:<math>\mu_3=8(k+3\lambda)\,</math>
:<math>\mu_4=12(k+2\lambda)^2+48(k+4\lambda)\,</math>

The ''n''th [[cumulant]] is

:<math>\kappa_n=2^{n-1}(n-1)!(k+n\lambda).\,</math>

Hence
:<math>\mu'_n = 2^{n-1}(n-1)!(k+n\lambda)+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \frac{(n-1)!2^{j-1}}{(n-j)!}(k+j\lambda )\mu'_{n-j}. </math>

=== Cumulative distribution function ===
Again using the relation between the central and noncentral chi-squared distributions, the [[cumulative distribution function]] (cdf) can be written as

:<math>P(x; k, \lambda ) = e^{-\lambda/2}\; \sum_{j=0}^\infty  \frac{(\lambda/2)^j}{j!} Q(x; k+2j)</math>

where <math>Q(x; k)\,</math> is the cumulative distribution function of the central chi-squared distribution with ''k'' degrees of freedom which is given by

:<math>Q(x;k)=\frac{\gamma(k/2,x/2)}{\Gamma(k/2)}\,</math>

:and where <math>\gamma(k,z)\,</math> is the [[lower incomplete gamma function]].

The [[Marcum Q-function]] <math>Q_M(a,b)</math> can also be used to represent the cdf.<ref>Nuttall, Albert H. (1975): ''[https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1055327/;jsessionid=B83CF5D65D889B2C82555368D5AEF7F5?arnumber=1055327 Some Integrals Involving the Q<sub>M</sub> Function]'', ''IEEE Transactions on Information Theory'', 21(1), 95–96, {{ISSN|0018-9448}}</ref>

:<math>P(x; k, \lambda) = 1 - Q_{\frac{k}{2}} \left( \sqrt{\lambda}, \sqrt{x} \right)</math>

When the degrees of freedom ''k'' is positive odd integer, we have a closed form expression for the complementary cumulative distribution function given by<ref name="Annamalai 2009">A. Annamalai, C. Tellambura and John Matyjas (2009). "A New Twist on the Generalized Marcum Q-Function ''Q''<sub>''M''</sub>(''a'',&nbsp;''b'') with Fractional-Order ''M'' and its Applications". ''2009 6th IEEE Consumer Communications and Networking Conference'', 1–5, {{ISBN|978-1-4244-2308-8}}</ref>

:<math>
\begin{align}
P(x; 2n+1, \lambda) &= 1 - Q_{n+1/2}(\sqrt{\lambda}, \sqrt{x}) \\
&= 1 - \left[ Q(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{\lambda}) + Q(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{\lambda}) + e^{-(x + \lambda)/2} \sum_{m=1}^n \left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{m/2-1/4} I_{m-1/2}(\sqrt{\lambda x}) \right],
\end{align}
</math>

where ''n'' is non-negative integer, ''Q'' is the [[Q-function|Gaussian Q-function]], and ''I'' is the modified Bessel function of first kind with half-integer order. The modified Bessel function of first kind with half-integer order in itself can be represented as a finite sum in terms of [[hyperbolic functions]].

In particular, for ''k'' = 1, we have

:<math>P(x; 1, \lambda) = 1 - \left[ Q(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{\lambda}) + Q(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{\lambda}) \right].</math>

Also, for ''k'' = 3, we have

:<math>P(x; 3, \lambda) = 1 - \left[ Q(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{\lambda}) + Q(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{\lambda}) + \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{\sinh (\sqrt{\lambda x})}{\sqrt{\lambda}} e^{-(x+\lambda)/2} \right].</math>

==== Approximation (including for quantiles) ====
Abdel-Aty derives (as "first approx.") a non-central [[Wilson–Hilferty transformation]]:<ref>{{cite journal |last=Abdel-Aty |first=S. |year=1954 |jstor=2332731 |title=Approximate Formulae for the Percentage Points and the Probability Integral of the Non-Central χ<sup>2</sup> Distribution |journal=[[Biometrika]] |volume=41 |issue= 3/4|pages=538–540 |doi=10.2307/2332731 }}</ref>

<math> \left(\frac{\chi'^2}{k+\lambda}\right)^{\frac 1 3}</math> is approximately [[Normal Distribution|normally distributed]], <math>\sim \mathcal{N}\left(1-\frac{2}{9f}, \frac{2}{9f} \right),</math> i.e.,

:<math> P(x; k, \lambda )\approx \Phi \left\{ \frac{\left(\frac{x}{k+\lambda}\right)^{1/3} - \left(1 - \frac{2}{9f}\right) }  {\sqrt{\frac{2}{9f}}  } \right\}, \text{where } \ f := \frac{(k+\lambda)^2}{k+2\lambda} = k + \frac{\lambda^2}{k+2\lambda},</math>

which is quite accurate and well adapting to the noncentrality. Also, <math>f = f(k,\lambda)</math> becomes <math>f = k</math> for <math>\lambda=0</math>, the [[Chi square distribution|(central) chi-squared]] case.

Sankaran discusses a number of [[Closed-form expression|closed form]] [[approximation]]s for the [[cumulative distribution function]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Sankaran |first=M. |year=1963 |doi=10.1093/biomet/50.1-2.199 |title=Approximations to the non-central chi-squared distribution |journal=[[Biometrika]] |volume=50 |issue=1–2 |pages=199–204 }}</ref> In an earlier paper, he derived and states the following approximation:<ref>{{cite journal |last=Sankaran |first=M. |year=1959 |title=On the non-central chi-squared distribution |journal=[[Biometrika]] |volume=46 |issue=1–2 |pages=235–237 |doi=10.1093/biomet/46.1-2.235 }}</ref>

:<math> P(x; k, \lambda ) \approx \Phi \left\{ \frac{(\frac{x}  {k + \lambda}) ^ h - (1 + h  p  (h - 1 - 0.5 (2 - h)  m  p))}  {h \sqrt{2p}  (1 + 0.5 m  p)} \right\}  </math>

where
:<math> \Phi \lbrace \cdot \rbrace \, </math> denotes the [[cumulative distribution function]] of the [[standard normal distribution]];
:<math> h = 1 - \frac{2}{3} \frac{(k+ \lambda)  (k+ 3  \lambda)}{(k+ 2  \lambda) ^ 2} \, ;</math>
:<math> p = \frac{k+ 2  \lambda}{(k+ \lambda) ^ 2} ;</math>
:<math> m = (h - 1)  (1 - 3  h) \, .</math>

This and other approximations are discussed in a later text book.<ref>Johnson et al. (1995) ''Continuous Univariate Distributions'' Section 29.8</ref>

More recently, since the CDF of non-central chi-squared distribution with odd degree of freedom can be exactly computed, the CDF for even degree of freedom can be approximated by exploiting the monotonicity and log-concavity properties of Marcum-Q function as

:<math> P(x; 2n, \lambda ) \approx \frac{1}{2}\left[ P(x; 2n - 1, \lambda) + P(x; 2n + 1, \lambda) \right].</math>

Another approximation that also serves as an upper bound is given by

:<math> P(x; 2n, \lambda ) \approx 1 - \left[ (1- P(x; 2n - 1, \lambda)) (1 - P(x; 2n + 1, \lambda)) \right]^{1/2}.</math>

For a given probability, these formulas are easily inverted to provide the corresponding approximation for <math> x</math>, to compute approximate quantiles.

== Related distributions ==
*If <math>V</math> is [[chi-squared distribution|chi-square]] distributed, <math>V \sim \chi_k^2</math>, then <math>V</math> is also non-central chi-square distributed: <math>V \sim {\chi'}^2_k(0)</math>
*A linear combination of independent noncentral chi-squared variables <math>\xi=\sum_i \lambda_i Y_i + c, \quad  Y_i \sim \chi'^2(m_i,\delta_i^2)</math>, is [[Generalized chi-squared distribution|generalized chi-square distributed]].
*If <math>V_1 \sim {\chi'}_{k_1}^2(\lambda)</math> and <math>V_2 \sim {\chi'}_{k_2}^2(0)</math> and <math>V_1</math> is independent of <math>V_2</math> then a [[noncentral F-distribution|noncentral ''F''-distributed]] variable is developed as <math>\frac{V_1/k_1}{V_2/k_2} \sim F'_{k_1,k_2}(\lambda)</math>
*If <math>J \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\left({\frac{1}{2}\lambda}\right)</math>, then <math>\chi_{k+2J}^2 \sim {\chi'}_k^2(\lambda)</math>
*If <math>V\sim{\chi'}^2_2(\lambda)</math>, then <math>\sqrt{V}</math> takes the [[Rice distribution]] with parameter <math>\sqrt{\lambda}</math>.
*Normal approximation:<ref>Muirhead (2005) pages 22–24 and problem 1.18.</ref> if <math>V \sim {\chi'}^2_k(\lambda)</math>, then <math>\frac{V-(k+\lambda)}{\sqrt{2(k+2\lambda)}}\to N(0,1)</math> in distribution as either <math>k\to\infty</math> or <math>\lambda\to\infty</math>.
*If <math>V_1 \sim {\chi'}^2_{k_1}(\lambda_1)</math>and <math>V_2 \sim {\chi'}^2_{k_2}(\lambda_2)</math>, where <math>V_1, V_2</math> are independent, then <math>W = (V_1+V_2) \sim {\chi'}^2_{k_1 + k_2}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)</math>.
*In general, for an independent finite set of <math>V_i \sim {\chi'}^2_{k_i}(\lambda_i)</math>, <math>i\in \{ 1, \ldots, N\}</math>, the sum of these non-central chi-square distributed random variables <math>Y = \sum_{i=1}^N V_i</math> has the distribution <math>Y \sim {\chi'}^2_{k_y}(\lambda_y)</math> where <math>k_y=\sum_{i=1}^N k_i</math>, <math>\lambda_y=\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i</math>. This can be seen using moment generating functions as follows: <math>M_Y(t) = M_{\sum_{i=1}^N V_i}(t) = \prod_{i=1}^N M_{V_i}(t)</math> by the independence of the <math>V_i</math> random variables. It remains to plug in the MGF for the non-central chi square distributions into the product and compute the new MGF&nbsp;– this is left as an exercise. Alternatively it can be seen via the interpretation in the background section above as sums of squares of independent normally distributed random variables with variances of 1 and the specified means.
* The ''complex noncentral chi-squared distribution'' has applications in radio communication and radar systems.{{citation needed|date=September 2020}} Let <math>z_1, \ldots, z_k</math> be independent scalar [[complex random variable]]s with noncentral circular symmetry, means of <math>\mu_i</math> and unit variances: <math> \operatorname{E} \left |z_i - \mu_i \right |^2 = 1 </math>. Then the real random variable <math>S = \sum_{i=1}^k \left |z_i \right | ^2</math> is distributed according to the complex noncentral chi-squared distribution, which is effectively a scaled (by 1/2) non-central <math>{\chi'}^2 </math> with twice the degrees of freedom and twice the noncentrality parameter:
:: <math> f_S(S) = \left( \frac {S}{\lambda} \right)^{(k-1)/2} e^{-(S + \lambda) }
 I_{k-1} (2 \sqrt {S\lambda} )</math>,
:where <math>\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^k \left |\mu_i \right |^2</math>.

=== Transformations ===

Sankaran (1963) discusses the transformations of the form
<math>z=[(X-b)/(k+\lambda)]^{1/2}</math>. He analyzes the expansions of the [[cumulant]]s of <math>z</math> up to the term <math>O((k+\lambda)^{-4})</math> and shows that the following choices of <math>b</math> produce reasonable results:

* <math>b=(k-1)/2</math> makes the second cumulant of <math>z</math> approximately independent of <math>\lambda</math>
* <math>b=(k-1)/3</math> makes the third cumulant of <math>z</math> approximately independent of <math>\lambda</math>
* <math>b=(k-1)/4</math> makes the fourth cumulant of <math>z</math> approximately independent of <math>\lambda</math>

Also, a simpler transformation <math>z_1 = (X-(k-1)/2)^{1/2}</math> can be used as a [[variance stabilizing transformation]] that produces a random variable with mean <math>(\lambda + (k-1)/2)^{1/2}</math> and variance <math>O((k+\lambda)^{-2})</math>.

Usability of these transformations may be hampered by the need to take the square roots of negative numbers.

== Occurrence and applications ==

=== Use in tolerance intervals ===
Two-sided normal [[regression analysis|regression]] [[tolerance interval]]s can be obtained based on the noncentral chi-squared distribution.<ref>{{cite journal| author=Derek S. Young| title=tolerance: An R Package for Estimating Tolerance Intervals| journal=Journal of Statistical Software|date=August 2010| volume=36| number=5| pages=1–39| issn=1548-7660| url=http://www.jstatsoft.org/v36/i05| access-date=19 February 2013}}, p.&nbsp;32</ref> This enables the calculation of a statistical interval within which, with some confidence level, a specified proportion of a sampled population falls.
